To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

selective attention resulted in activation at left hemisphere sites, whereas divided attention resulted in activation in both hemispheres, and executive function resulted in activation at frontal sites.

selective attention, divided attention and executive function, as measured in the context of language processing tasks, are associated with distinctive patterns of neural activation in widely distributed but distinctive neural systems.

(1) Selective attention in language-processing tasks is associated with increased activation at parietal sites, and (2) executive function in language-processing tasks, which requires the ability to switch between different cognitive operations, is associated with increased frontal lobe activation.

the functional architecture of attention in the context of language processing and provides evidence that the neural mechanisms underlying the control of selective and divided attention are differentially engaged during language-processing tasks.

selective attention, divided attention and executive function all have a role in language processing.

the functional neuroanatomy of the components of attention in language processing is not a simple matter of one component of attention having one location in the brain, but rather that the components of attention have different functional neural architectures, and that these architectures involve widely distributed but distinct cortical systems.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the functional architecture for components of attentional control is distributed across multiple cortical sites, and that this distributed system is organized into a network of functionally specific subsystems, each of which involves distinct cortical regions.
attentional control is not a unitary phenomenon but rather is composed of multiple functional components.

the control of language-processing tasks is associated with a distributed network of brain regions, and the specific pattern of activation within this network varies as a function of the specific demands of the language-processing task.
The main takeaway from our work is that

attention in the context of language processing is a multifaceted phenomenon that involves the engagement of widely distributed neural systems, and that different aspects of attentional processing are associated with different neural systems.
the neural systems that support attentional control in the language domain are widely distributed, with different aspects of control involving different cortical systems.
there are specific neural systems that support the control of attentional processes, and that these neural systems are not simply a reflection of more general attentional mechanisms.
